title: Monera and Bacteria

mcqs.question: The smallest known living cell is:
The cell wall of most bacteria is made of:
Gram-positive bacteria appear what colour after Gram staining?
The primary asexual reproduction method in bacteria is:

notes: Kingdom Monera: prokaryotic organisms (no membrane-bound nucleus); includes bacteria, cyanobacteria (blue-green algae), mycoplasma, and archaebacteria.
Bacterial cell: capsule (slime layer) → cell wall (peptidoglycan) → plasma membrane → cytoplasm; 70S ribosomes; naked circular DNA (nucleoid); may have pili, fimbriae, flagella, mesosomes.
Shapes: cocci (spherical), bacilli (rod), spirilla/spirochaetes (spiral). Arrangements: diplococci, streptococci, staphylococci.
Mode of nutrition: autotrophic (photoautotrophs, chemoautotrophs) and heterotrophic (saprophytes, parasites).
Bacterial growth: lag → log (exponential) → stationary → death phases; reproduction by binary fission (asexual) and by conjugation/transformation/transduction (genetic exchange).
Cyanobacteria: blue-green algae; photosynthetic; Nostoc, Anabaena (fix atmospheric nitrogen); important in rice paddies as biofertilisers.
Gram staining: Gram-positive (thick peptidoglycan, purple) vs Gram-negative (thin peptidoglycan + outer membrane, pink).
confusion: Bacteria are prokaryotic: they have no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles.
Cyanobacteria are bacteria (prokaryotes), NOT algae; they fix nitrogen but are not "true" algae.
Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall; it is the smallest known living cell.
Archaea differ from Bacteria in cell wall (no peptidoglycan) and membrane lipids; they live in extreme environments.
Binary fission produces two genetically identical daughter cells; conjugation transfers DNA but does not increase cell number.
Gram-positive bacteria have a THICK peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative have a THIN layer plus an outer LPS membrane (more resistant to many antibiotics).
practice: Draw and label a typical bacterium (capsule, wall, membrane, cytoplasm, nucleoid, ribosomes, flagellum, pili).
Describe the bacterial growth curve (4 phases).
Explain the Gram-staining procedure and differentiate Gram +ve and -ve.
Tabulate the three modes of bacterial nutrition with examples.
State the economic and ecological importance of bacteria (5 points).
universalFacts: Bacteria are the oldest life form on Earth (~3.5 billion years).
A single bacterial cell can divide in ~20 minutes under optimal conditions (E. coli).
More than 99% of the organisms on Earth are prokaryotes.
Rhizobium in legume root nodules fixes atmospheric N₂ into usable ammonia (symbiotic nitrogen fixation).
examples: Escherichia coli — rod-shaped, Gram-negative, model organism for genetics.
Lactobacillus — rod, used in curd/cheese making (lactic acid fermentation).
Nostoc / Anabaena — cyanobacteria, filamentous, nitrogen-fixing in rice fields.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae — smallest living cell (no cell wall), causes atypical pneumonia.
practiceQuestions: Differentiate the four phases of the bacterial growth curve.
Explain the Gram-staining test and its significance.
What are the different shapes of bacteria with one example each?
State the ecological importance of bacteria (decomposition, nitrogen cycle, symbiosis).
formulas: Binary fission: 1 cell → 2 identical daughter cells (asexual)
Growth curve: N(t) = N₀ × 2ⁿ (n = number of generations in log phase)
Gram +ve: thick peptidoglycan → retains crystal violet (purple); Gram -ve: thin + LPS → pink (safranin)
keyPoints: Monera = prokaryotic: no true nucleus, 70S ribosomes, circular DNA.
Shapes: cocci, bacilli, spirilla; arrangements: diplo-, strepto-, staphylo-.
Nutrition: autotrophic (photo/chemo) + heterotrophic (saprophytes, parasites).
Growth curve: lag, log, stationary, death.
Binary fission = asexual reproduction; conjugation/transformation/transduction = genetic exchange.
Cyanobacteria: photosynthetic + nitrogen-fixing (Nostoc, Anabaena).
Gram stain: +ve (purple, thick wall) vs -ve (pink, thin wall + LPS).
enrichedContent.summary: Kingdom Monera comprises prokaryotic organisms: bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma, and archaebacteria. Bacteria show diverse shapes, nutrition, and reproduction (binary fission + genetic exchange). The growth curve (lag, log, stationary, death) and Gram staining are fundamental microbiology tools. Cyanobacteria fix nitrogen and photosynthesise. Bacteria are ecologically indispensable as decomposers, nitrogen fixers, and symbionts, and economically vital in food, industry, and medicine.
